exam: What is the first step in managing a child with a suspected dental abscess? — Identify airway risk, then drain or refer.
How would you differentiate a dental abscess from cellulitis? — Look for fluctuation, localized pain, and a single tooth involved.
Why is clindamycin preferred in penicillin‑allergic patients? — Covers anaerobes and resistant streptococci.
What red flag would prompt immediate ENT referral? — Difficulty breathing or swallowing.
How does HIV infection alter the presentation of a dental abscess? — May present with less pain, more rapid spread, higher risk of sepsis.
What is the rationale for using a point‑of‑care ultrasound in low‑resource settings? — It visualises fluid collection and guides safe aspiration.
ai.title: Dental Abscess in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A dental abscess is a localized collection of pus from a tooth or surrounding tissues, often secondary to untreated decay or trauma. Clinical focus is on prompt drainage, infection control and prevention of systemic spread, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Radiograph shows radiolucency at root apex
sections.p: A dental abscess is a focal purulent infection arising from a tooth root or pericoronal tissues. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple imaging when available.

t.b: Absence of radiolucency does not rule out early abscess
May miss deep abscesses if not visualised

b: Stage I – localized pain, no systemic signs
Stage II – swelling, fever <38.5 °C, mild trismus
Stage III – severe swelling, high fever >39 °C, trismus, possible airway compromise
sections.p: Staging guides urgency and treatment. In low‑resource settings, clinical staging is most practical.

b: Traumatic injury to primary or permanent teeth
sections.p: In East Africa, untreated dental caries and trauma are predominant. Other contributors include poor oral hygiene, malnutrition and HIV‑related immunosuppression.

b: Altered mental status if sepsis develops
sections.p: Children present with acute pain, swelling, fever and difficulty chewing. Systemic signs may be subtle.
Use bedside tests; advanced imaging is optional.

t.b: Normal WCC does not exclude abscess
Normal values do not rule out localized infection
Negative cultures common in localized abscess

b: Prompt drainage – needle aspiration or incision and drainage
Antibiotics: amoxicillin‑clavulanate or clindamycin if penicillin‑allergic
Referral to ENT if airway compromise
sections.p: Treat the source, control infection and monitor for spread.

t.b: Avoid in patients with renal impairment

b: Re‑examine in 48–72 h for residual swelling
Schedule dental extraction or root canal
sections.p: Ensure definitive dental care and educate on oral hygiene.
